To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
swelling of S49 wild-type mouse lymphoma cells causes an increase in the intracellular concentrations of cAMP and Ca2+.
swelling of mouse lymphoma cells induces rapid accumulation of intracellar cAMP, which is attenuated by beta-blockade.
swelling of S49 mouse lymphocytes in hypotonic medium results in a rapid accumulation of intracelluar cAMP and calcium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of cAMP metabolism in the S49 lymphoma cell.
the effects of cellular volume on the metabolism of calcium and cyclic AMP in S49 mouse wild-type lymphoma cells and the possible role of calcium in regulating cyclic AMP metabolism in these cells.
the role of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) second messenger in regulating the volume regulatory response of S49 wild-type and variant mouse lymphoma cells to hyposmotic stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
swelling of S49 mouse lymphocytes in hyposmotic medium results in a rapid accumulation of calcium and cAMP.
the swelling of S49 wild-type mouse lymphoma cells causes a rapid and significant increase in intracellular c-AMP and calcium.
the accumulation of cAMP and Ca2+ in S49 cells following swelling is not due to a single mechanism, but is likely to be a complex response involving multiple mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
swelling of S49 cells stimulates the production of cAMP, which is mediated by an adenosine receptor and a calcium-dependent protein kinase.
swelling stimulates cAMP and Ca2+ accumulation, and that this effect is mediated by the beta-adrenoceptor and is not dependent on extracellular Ca2+.
swelling-induced calcium and cAMP responses in mouse lymphoma cells occur rapidly and involve a complex interplay of multiple mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
swelling of cells in a defined medium can stimulate rapid accumulation of cAMP and that the accumulation of cAMP can be modulated by several pharmacological agents.
the cAMP response is mediated through a beta-adrenergic receptor.

the swelling-activated calcium and cAMP responses in S49 wild-type cells occur in the absence of extracellular calcium, sodium, and magnesium, but are dependent on the presence of extracellular chloride.
